section: How the Blog and Dashboards Connect
text:
How the Blog and Dashboards Connect
Every analysis on this blog links to an interactive dashboard where you can explore the data with your own filters. For example, here’s a simple summary of event counts by quarter:


Code
library(ggplot2)

events <- data.frame(
  period = c("Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"),
  count = c(120, 185, 210, 175)
)

ggplot(events, aes(x = period, y = count, fill = period)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Event Count by Quarter", x = "Period", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

title: Why event-driven analytics?
text: Traditional analytics relies on periodic snapshots — daily reports, weekly aggregations, monthly summaries. This approach loses the sequence of events and makes it impossible to answer questions like “what happened between Tuesday and Thursday that caused the spike?”

title: Why event-driven analytics?
text:
Event-driven advantages
Event-driven analytics preserves the full timeline. With event data you can:

Track user journeys step by step through a funnel
Detect anomalies in real time as they happen
Replay history to understand what led to an outcome
Build flexible aggregations at any time granularity

title: Why event-driven analytics?
text:
When to use event-driven analytics
Event-driven approaches work best when timing and sequence matter — user behavior analysis, operational monitoring, IoT sensor data, and financial transaction tracking.
For static, slowly-changing data (annual reports, census data), traditional snapshot approaches are simpler and sufficient.

title: Event dashboard design
text: Event dashboards differ from traditional BI dashboards. They need to handle temporal data, streaming updates, and user-driven exploration.

title: Event dashboard design
text:
Key principles
Start with a question, not a chart. Every dashboard panel should answer a specific question: “How many events occurred this quarter?” or “Which event types are trending?”
Time is the primary axis. Event data is inherently temporal. The x-axis should almost always be time, with the ability to zoom in and out.
Filters drive exploration. Users need to slice data by event type, source, time period, and custom attributes. Shiny’s reactive model is ideal for this.

title: What Are Events?
text: An event is a record of something that happened at a specific point in time. Every click, transaction, sensor reading, or status change can be captured as an event.

title: What Are Events?
text:
Anatomy of an Event
At minimum, an event has:

Timestamp — when it happened
Type — what kind of event it is (e.g., page_view, purchase, alert)
Payload — the data associated with the event



Code
event <- list(
  timestamp = Sys.time(),
  type = "page_view",
  payload = list(
    user_id = "u_12345",
    page = "/dashboard",
    duration_seconds = 45
  )
)

str(event)


List of 3
 $ timestamp: POSIXct[1:1], format: "2026-05-02 00:37:18"
 $ type     : chr "page_view"
 $ payload  :List of 3
  ..$ user_id         : chr "u_12345"
  ..$ page            : chr "/dashboard"
  ..$ duration_seconds: num 45

title: What Are Events?
text:
Why Events Matter
Traditional analytics asks “what is the current state?” Event analytics asks “what happened, in what order, and why?” This shift unlocks temporal analysis, funnel tracking, and real-time monitoring.
